text:
Who you can nominate

You can nominate anyone who is serving, or has served, in the Merchant Navy or fishing fleets of the United Kingdom, Isle of Man, the Channel Islands or the British Overseas Territories.

The nominee must not be told that they are being nominated.

Successful nominations have come from across the maritime sector, including the fishing sector, with meritorious contributions recognised at all levels.

Recipients of the medal have included junior deck crew, early‑career seafarers, mid‑level technical specialists, shore‑based professionals, senior officers and captains. We have had recipients across a wide age range, from people in their twenties through to people in their seventies.

Meritorious service may be shown through either:

sustained contributions built up over a career

a single significant act

To be considered for the Merchant Navy Medal, the meritorious contribution should include actions that have taken place within recent years.

Where a nomination focuses on a single significant act, this should ideally have occurred within the last few years.

Where a nomination highlights a range of contributions over time, at least some of these should also be recent.

Examples of meritorious contributions in the maritime sector

These are examples of the sort of contributions for which the medal is awarded.

A successful nomination would demonstrate what the nominee did to make these things happen and what the results of their actions were.

Do not copy and paste these examples - your nomination should describe what the nominee actually did.

Examples of meritorious contributions

Showing exceptional commitment to seafarer welfare by strengthening onboard safety practices and maintaining consistent support during challenging operational periods.

Championing fairness and inclusion within the maritime workforce, creating networks and support structures that improve opportunities for under‑represented groups.

Leading the development of innovative vessel‑tracking and operational methods that enhance safety and efficiency in busy waters.

Providing dedicated service to remote coastal communities, ensuring access to vital transport, medical care and essential supplies.

Delivering sustained leadership in modernising onboard systems and training, resulting in improved operational safety and crew capability.

Supporting the development of maritime skills and capability through education, training or mentoring.

Enhancing navigational safety through the modernisation of critical coastal infrastructure and maintaining continuity of operations during severe weather.

Demonstrating exceptional bravery during a complex offshore rescue operation, repeatedly returning to hazardous conditions to recover survivors and support emergency teams.

Answering the nomination questions

The nomination form asks you to tell us:

about the person’s job and the situation before they made a difference

what they did to make things better

the result of what they did – what lasting impact did their actions have?

Use the tips below to make your case clear and compelling.

These examples are illustrative only and should not be copied directly.

1. The person’s job and the issues they faced (150 words)

We want to understand the situation the person faced in their role before they took actions to make a difference.

Tell us about the context of their work and any challenges - for example, relating to:

size of team

resources

environment

urgency of tasks

difficult conditions

taking extra responsibility

starting something new, perhaps with no resources or with no previous experience

2. Actions of the nominee (400 words)

Tell us what they did to make a difference.

This could either be:

several examples across time to show sustained merit

one major event / project that made an exceptional change

Show why their achievements were significant given any unfavourable circumstances described. For example, did they influence the safety culture, training, welfare or showed innovation?

Focus on how they personally contributed - specific actions, decisions and how they demonstrated leadership.

Make clear why the nominee is an ‘outstanding example to others’. How did the nominee’s actions exceed what’s expected for their role?

Avoid vague statements like “they are hard-working” or “they are well-respected” without examples.

Do not just list awards or career history. Explain what they did, why it was exceptional and how they are an example to others.

3. Results and impact (200 words)

Explain what changed because of the nominee’s actions.

Who benefited (for example, crews, cadets, the company, sector) and how?

Include facts and figures wherever possible - for example ‘reduced incidents by 30%’, ‘trained 50 new seafarers’, ‘saved £100,000 through efficiency improvements’, ‘15 cadets mentored’, ‘policy used by two partner companies’, ‘project adoption by industry’.

Highlight specific achievements and lasting impact/improvements or spread to other companies/parts of the sector/within their organisation.

Writing your nomination

A good nomination

Have a clear idea of why you are nominating someone before you start writing the nomination.

Nominations should focus on achievements that are remarkable.

Demonstrate how the nominee has gone above and beyond, making a real difference and setting an outstanding example for others.

Use plain English and short sentences, keeping your nomination clear and concise.

Focus on merit, not on length of service.

Be specific by describing what the nominee did, not just their qualities.

Focus on the impact of their actions.

Make clear what the specific achievements are.

Avoid jargon and technical terms.

Include facts and figures wherever possible.

Demonstrate sustained impact by including examples from different periods or projects to show ongoing commitment. If one event is highlighted, make clear why it was exceptional and how it reflects the nominee’s wider contribution.

What to avoid

Do not just list the nominee’s career history or achievements.

Do not focus on long service as this is not a long service award.

Do not use vague statements or generic praise (for example, “they are well respected”) without giving clear examples.

Do not submit nominations that simply describe someone doing their job well - focus on what is truly exceptional.

Example of a good nomination

This nomination is good because it:

focuses on the nominee’s personal actions and impact

explains the context clearly

emphasises the significance of the contributions

does not just list roles or rely solely on the length of service

What issues did the nominee face in their role?

Chief Officer Anita Patel served on a cargo vessel, leading a small crew through a particularly demanding shipping season. Her role required her to oversee daily operations, ensure the safety and wellbeing of all crew members, and manage complex logistics, often with limited resources and under tight deadlines.

The ship regularly faced unpredictable weather and long periods at sea, which placed additional pressure on both the team and Chief Officer Patel. Despite these challenges, she was quick to notice that many seafarers struggled with feelings of isolation and uncertainty about where to seek help.

When she later transitioned to a shore-based role, she recognised that these issues were widespread and not limited to her own vessel. Motivated by what she had observed, she took on the responsibility of creating a new support programme for seafarers, starting from zero, with no existing framework or resources to build upon.

What did the nominee do?

After recognising the difficulties faced by crew members, she made a point of listening to their concerns and understanding the issues that affected their wellbeing. Rather than simply carrying out her usual duties, she took the initiative to design a support programme that addressed the real needs of seafarers. She spent her own time developing resources and running drop-in sessions, making sure that help was available to anyone who needed it.

She also created easy-to-read guides for new joiners, ensuring that even those unfamiliar with the organisation could access support. She worked closely with other departments to make the programme available across different ships, showing a commitment to improving the lives of seafarers beyond her immediate team.

Furthermore, she shared their approach with other companies, allowing the benefits of the programme to reach even more people in the maritime sector. Her actions were not part of her formal responsibilities but stemmed from a desire to make a lasting difference for others.

What was the result / impact of the nominee’s action?

As a result of her efforts, seafarers felt more supported and confident, both at sea and ashore. In the first year, over 50 crew members used the new support programme, and feedback showed that people felt less isolated and more able to ask for help. The scheme was adopted by two other companies, extending its positive impact beyond her own organisation. Reports of wellbeing concerns dropped by 40%, and the programme became a model for supporting seafarers across the sector. These outstanding results and effort, make Chief Officer Patel deserving of the Merchant Navy Medal for Meritorious Service.

Because of these actions, new recruits reported that they felt more supported and confident. Three other ships adopted the mentoring scheme. Reports of workplace concerns dropped by 50%, and more women and LGBT+ seafarers joined the company.

After the delivery of the new joiners brief and workshops, reported bullying cases fell by a third across two vessels. Two partner companies adopted the toolkit the nominee developed. New joiner surveys showed higher confidence about reporting concerns.

Example of a poorly written nomination

This nomination is poor because it does not explain what the nominee personally did or why it was exceptional. It’s just a list of job history and general praise.

What issues did the nominee face in their role?

Captain Johnson has worked as a Chief Officer for several years, responsible for overseeing cargo operations, maintaining safety standards and ensuring compliance with company procedures. His duties include supervising crew, managing paperwork, and coordinating with port authorities. He is known for being reliable, and getting the job done. He is hardworking and respected by everyone.

What did the nominee do?

With more than 30 years of experience at sea, Captain Johnson has steadily progressed to a senior position through tireless dedication and always going the extra mile. Throughout his 40-year career, he has obtained numerous qualifications (a full list is provided below) and held a variety of important roles, including Chief Officer and Master on several vessels (a full list of his positions is provided below). His impressive record includes extensive service on different ship types and a long list of professional achievements. As demonstrated by the positions held and his long career, Captain Johnson is very committed to his work, and he enjoys the respect from colleagues at all levels.

What was the result / impact of the nominee’s action?

Captain Johnson’s work is truly outstanding and has made a tremendous difference to the lives of the countless people they worked with throughout the years. Because of this they are wholly deserving of this prestigious award.

Support letters

Each nomination must include at least 2 letters of support from people who know the nominee’s work well.

Support letters should be written by people who have direct experience of the nominee’s work or impact. This could include managers, colleagues, industry leaders.

A good support letter should:

give specific examples of the nominee’s achievements

highlight the difference the nominee has made, using facts, figures, or stories where possible

add new information or perspectives, rather than simply repeating the main nomination

The letter should be concise, ideally no more than one page.

Letters that simply offer general praise or repeat the nomination are less helpful. The best letters provide clear, first-hand evidence of the nominee’s exceptional service and impact.

Make a nomination

The easiest way to make a nomination is using the online nomination form.

The form allows you to save your progress, so you can start a nomination and come back to it later if you need more time.
